FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A01
Passing the written test does not by itself issue a learner's permit; the permit is issued only after every other requirement is met and every required document is provided [A01].
Why it matters: The test is one condition among several.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A01
Most motor vehicle crashes are caused by the actions or errors of the driver, and any motorist can drive safely through care, courtesy and caution and by modeling proper behavior [A01].
Why it matters: The handbook pins crash causation on driver behavior.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A01
A new permit holder should begin practicing in an empty parking lot or on lightly traveled roads to build basic car control before moving to busier roads as skills improve [A01].
Why it matters: Start where traffic is lightest.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A01
When a slow driver has traffic piling up behind, the law requires that driver to move to the roadside once it is safe and let the vehicles behind go past [A01].
Why it matters: Letting traffic by is a legal duty, not a courtesy.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A01
Hands belong on the steering wheel at the nine and three or the eight and four clock positions, with hand over hand steering used for turns, while practicing left and right turns, smooth braking and controlled starts and stops [A01].
Why it matters: Hand position is a commonly tested basic.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A01
Driver readiness before moving means adjusting the seat, adjusting all mirrors, testing the foot and parking brakes, adjusting and fastening the safety belt, locking the doors and turning on the headlights [A01].
Why it matters: Six checklist steps, headlights included.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A01
Even with ideal road and vehicle conditions and a fully alert driver, stopping a vehicle takes a great distance, and a stop requires that you see and recognize the danger before anything else happens [A01].
Why it matters: Recognition is the first of the four stopping events.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A02
After the driver recognizes danger, the brain must tell the foot to brake, the foot must move to the pedal and operate it, and the brakes must work correctly before the vehicle stops [A02].
Why it matters: Three mechanical steps follow recognition.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A02
Reaction distance is the distance traveled from the moment you see danger until you step on the brake, the average driver needs about three quarters of a second to apply the brakes, and higher speed means more distance covered before braking begins [A02].
Why it matters: Three quarters of a second is the handbook figure for reaction time.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A02
Braking distance is the distance traveled from the moment the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops, and it becomes much longer on wet, icy or gravel roads [A02].
Why it matters: Braking distance depends on the road surface.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A02
When rain first begins, oil, rubber, dirt and water mix to make the road especially slippery, which increases braking distance [A02].
Why it matters: The first minutes of rain are the slickest.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A02
The law requires a turn signal to be given not less than one hundred feet before turning or changing lanes, and signaling three to five seconds ahead satisfies that requirement [A02].
Why it matters: One hundred feet in law, three to five seconds in practice.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A02
Pressing the brakes warns drivers behind that you intend to slow or stop, and if the directional or brake lights fail you are required to give hand signals instead and have the lights repaired at once [A02].
Why it matters: Hand signals are mandatory, not optional, when lights fail.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A02
Many crashes happen while a vehicle is turning left, and most of them would be avoided if the driver made the turn properly [A02].
Why it matters: Left turns are the handbook's highlighted crash scenario.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A02
Approaching a left turn, signal three to five seconds in advance, slow gradually while checking the rearview mirror to confirm the driver behind understood, make sure no bicyclist or vehicle behind is trying to pass on your left, and on a multilane road be in the left lane well ahead of the turn without moving suddenly from the right lane [A02].
Why it matters: The approach steps for a left turn are frequently tested.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A02
At the left turn itself, wait until no vehicles are oncoming, position the vehicle within one foot of the centerline when safe, and keep the wheels straight until you actually turn so a rear end hit will not push you into oncoming traffic [A02].
Why it matters: Straight wheels while waiting is a safety detail examiners test.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A02
Any oncoming vehicle or bicyclist has the right-of-way over a left turning driver, and pedestrians crossing the street you are turning into must also be yielded to [A02].
Why it matters: Two separate yields apply during a left turn.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A02
Once the road is clear, complete the left turn at a proper speed keeping to the right of the center line, then check the rearview mirror and center the vehicle in its lane [A02].
Why it matters: Finishing the turn has its own two steps.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A03
Before a left turn the driver searches the intersection to the right, the front and the left, and enters the new street just to the right of its center line [A03].
Why it matters: The search order for a left turn begins on the right.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A03
On the approach to a right turn keep the vehicle roughly three feet from the road's right edge, never swing out to the left first, and put the signal on three to five seconds ahead while slowing and checking the mirror [A03].
Why it matters: No swing out to the left before a right turn.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A03
Before a right turn the driver searches the intersection left, front, right and then quickly left again, stays alert for bicyclists or pedestrians on the right side, must yield to any of them, and keeps close to the right side of the lane while turning [A03].
Why it matters: The right turn search ends with a second look left.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F22 | anchor: A03
When turning into a street with more than one lane in your direction, turn into the nearest lane, and then follow the multilane rule of driving on the right unless passing or turning [A03].
Why it matters: Nearest lane first, then keep right.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F23 | anchor: A03
A visual search pattern is an orderly, repeating way of looking for hazards in every direction, including pedestrians, bicyclists and other vulnerable users, so the driver notices changing conditions in and around the intended path [A03].
Why it matters: The search pattern is a habit, not a single glance.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F24 | anchor: A03
The four second method leaves enough room to stop quickly behind the vehicle ahead, and when the road is poor, visibility is poor or speeds are higher the gap should grow beyond four seconds [A03].
Why it matters: Four seconds is the minimum, not the rule for every condition.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F25 | anchor: A04
To measure four second spacing, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a checkpoint such as a sign, driveway, pole or parked vehicle, count seconds until your vehicle reaches it, and fewer than four seconds means you are following too closely and must drop back [A04].
Why it matters: The counting method is a likely test scenario.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F26 | anchor: A04
An easy way to count seconds for following distance is to say one thousand one, one thousand two and so on [A04].
Why it matters: The counting phrase is the handbook's own tip.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F27 | anchor: A04
The maximum speed for any vehicle on all Vermont roads is fifty miles per hour or as posted, and on a Vermont interstate the maximum is sixty-five miles per hour or as posted [A04].
Why it matters: Fifty statewide, sixty-five on the interstate.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F28 | anchor: A04
The law requires a vehicle to be under control at all times and driven at a speed that is reasonable for the dangers present, so at intersections, on curves, in heavy traffic, through construction zones, in bad weather and near pedestrians or bicyclists you must slow to a speed safe for conditions [A04].
Why it matters: The posted limit is never a guarantee of a safe speed.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F29 | anchor: A04
Many crashes are caused by driving too fast for conditions, and the handbook warns that even ten miles per hour can sometimes be an unsafe speed [A04].
Why it matters: Even very low speeds can be too fast.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F30 | anchor: A04
On every road, pedestrians, bicyclists and other traffic that are already inside an intersection have the right-of-way over a driver arriving at it [A04].
Why it matters: Whoever is already in the intersection goes first.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F31 | anchor: A04
Nearing an intersection with a yield right-of-way sign, you must travel slowly enough to stop if necessary and enter only when the way is clear [A04].
Why it matters: Yield means be ready to stop completely.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F32 | anchor: A04
At a four way stop the first vehicle to arrive has the right-of-way, and when two vehicles arrive at about the same time from different directions the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right [A04].
Why it matters: First to arrive, then yield to the right.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F33 | anchor: A04
A driver turning left must yield to all oncoming traffic, because any vehicle coming toward you, whether a motor vehicle or a bicyclist, has the right-of-way [A04].
Why it matters: Oncoming bicycles have the same right-of-way as cars.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F34 | anchor: A04
A driver coming onto a road out of a driveway, an alley, a parking lot or the stem of a T intersection gives the right-of-way to every vehicle already traveling on that road [A04].
Why it matters: Entering traffic always yields to through traffic.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F35 | anchor: A04
Before entering any intersection you must search in all directions and make sure you have a clear path through it [A04].
Why it matters: Searching all directions is required every time.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0029]

Misconceptions:
- Signaling at the last moment is fine as long as the signal is on: false, the law requires the signal not less than one hundred feet ahead, which three to five seconds of signaling covers.
- Turning the wheels toward the turn while waiting to go left is efficient: false, keep the wheels straight so a rear end collision cannot push you into oncoming traffic.
- Four seconds is always enough following distance: false, poor roads, poor visibility and higher speeds call for more than four seconds.
- The posted limit is the safe speed: false, conditions such as curves, construction, weather and pedestrians require a slower speed, and even ten miles per hour can be unsafe.
- At a four way stop the driver on the right always goes first: false, the first vehicle to arrive goes first; the yield to the right applies only when vehicles arrive together.

Mnemonics:
- Nine and three or eight and four: the two recommended hand positions on the wheel.
- See, think, move, work: the four things that must happen to stop, from seeing the danger to the brakes working.
- Right front left for a left, left front right and left again for a right: the two intersection search orders.
- Fifty on the road, sixty-five on the interstate: Vermont's two maximum speeds unless posted lower.

Glossary:
- Reaction distance: the distance a vehicle travels between the moment the driver sees danger and the moment the brake is pressed
- Braking distance: the distance a vehicle travels from the moment the brakes are applied until it stops
- Four second method: counting the seconds between the vehicle ahead passing a checkpoint and your own vehicle reaching it, with four or more being safe
- Visual search pattern: an orderly, repeating way of scanning every direction for hazards and changes near the intended path
- Yield right-of-way sign: an intersection sign requiring a speed slow enough to stop and entry only when the way is clear
